target_claim_or_section: §5 Re-vetting as verification of change; 05 §5 item 3; 17 XRI-003
challenge: The package treats the 180-day re-review as a requirement that an auditor must agree to waive. No IRS rule sets a 180-day re-review. 4966 and Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance turns on status at the time of the grant (TEOS/BMF/letter, unless published notice or knowledge of a change). The 180-day cycle is a sponsor policy (PR #88 / Unbound design). So the real gate is a sponsor board or policy amendment plus documented reliance, not auditor acceptance. Comparing $482k with $115k is also a straw man, because the legal floor is transaction-time status plus 4966(d)(4) checks. The '4x saving' measures a self-imposed cost, not a competitive advantage over incumbents that may not run full re-reviews at all.
evidence: Rev. Proc. 2018-32 (IRB 2018-23), which supersedes Rev. Proc. 2011-33: grantors may rely on TEOS/EO BMF for 4966 grants, except after published notice or knowledge. IRS page 'Reliance criteria for private foundations and sponsoring organizations that maintain DAFs' sets no periodic re-review requirement. No primary source for a 180-day rule is cited in 02, 04, 05 or 17.
proposed_change: Recast HYP-005/OQ-004: (a) identify where the 180-day rule comes from (Unbound policy, a sponsor policy or an auditor expectation); (b) frame it as a sponsor policy choice backed by Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance; (c) re-baseline CLM-005 against what incumbents actually do (transaction-time Pub 78/BMF check), not against a full re-review.

target_claim_or_section: §5 'Every input a sponsor needs for the legal minimum ... is free and redistributable'; 02 §4
challenge: This is overstated. 4966(c)(2) exempts only 170(b)(1)(A) organizations other than 'disqualified supporting organizations'. Under 4966(d)(4), that term covers every Type III non-functionally-integrated SO, plus any Type I or Type III SO where the donor or advisor controls a supported organization. Donor control cannot be determined from IRS public files. It needs a grantee certification or donor attestation (Notice 2006-109 reliance approach), which is charity-provided or donor-provided evidence and not shareable. Other gaps public data cannot close: churches not required to seek recognition, group-exemption subordinates (Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance excludes subordinates not separately listed), foreign grantees needing an equivalency determination or ER, and private non-operating foundations needing ER. In 4966 terms the 'legal minimum' is not fully public-data.
evidence: IRC 4966(c)(2) and (d)(4); Notice 2006-109 §4 (certification reliance); the IRS reliance-criteria page warns that Type III NFI grants are 'subject to more restrictive rules'; the Rev. Proc. 2018-32 summary says reliance does not extend to subordinates not separately listed. 02 §4 already admits churches and subordinates need proprietary lists.
proposed_change: Add a 4966 decision tree to 04 that lists each check needing non-public evidence: SO donor-control certification, ER, equivalency determination, church and subordinate status. Route those checks to the sponsor-specific or charity-provided classes. Re-estimate the share of grants (and the exception rate in 05 and 09 E08/E10) that need non-public evidence.

target_claim_or_section: §2 MD-6 'not a TPSP if no payment origination (counsel)'; 05 RC-10 and §5 item 4
challenge: This mis-frames the Nacha test. TPSP status turns on function, not on who originates. Any party that performs an ACH processing function for an Originator, ODFI or RDFI is a TPSP, and that explicitly includes creating files even if it never transmits them. A licensed platform that builds the sponsor's NACHA payment file is a TPSP almost by construction, even with the sponsor as Originator. A hybrid exception service (MD-7) that holds or releases payments, or a service that sends files to the ODFI, is more clearly a TPSP. It becomes a Third-Party Sender if the sponsor's origination agreement is with Unbound and not with the ODFI. So treating RC-10 ($44k) as conditional and 'removable' is optimistic. The OQ-009 question also asks the wrong thing: it should be 'which TPSP obligations, and who audits them', not 'whether Unbound is a TPSP'.
evidence: Nacha 'Third Parties in the ACH Network': a TPSP 'provides services related to ACH processing on behalf of another party; may or may not transmit entries directly'. Nacha consulting material and the UMACHA glossary list 'file creation' as a TPSP function. TPSPs and TPSs must complete an annual Rules Compliance Audit for the functions they perform for a DFI or TPS.
proposed_change: Assume TPSP status whenever the platform generates ACH or positive-pay files or controls release timing. Move RC-10's audit portion to 'contractually required' for MD-6, MD-7 and MD-5. Narrow OQ-009 to the Third-Party Sender question and to how audit duties are allocated.

target_claim_or_section: §6 fraud row 'Callback to aged contacts; bank-change holds ... INFERENCE (Nacha false-pretenses)'; E11/E19
challenge: The model treats fraud prevention as an optional design lever that cuts losses by 70%. Since the Nacha risk-management rules (Phase 1 on 2026-03-20; Phase 2 practically on 2026-06-22), every non-consumer Originator (the sponsor), every TPSP and every Third-Party Sender, whatever its volume, must have risk-based processes to detect entries authorized under false pretenses, reviewed at least annually. That is a mandatory control with fixed review and documentation labour per sponsor and per vendor. It is missing from the sponsor-level events E21-E23 and from the MD-6/MD-7 cost lines.
evidence: Nacha 'Risk Management Topics - Fraud Monitoring Phase 2': removes the volume threshold for non-consumer Originators/TPSPs/TPSs; effective 2026-06-19 (practically 2026-06-22); annual review required. Nacha news 2026-03-20 'New Nacha risk management rules now in effect'.
proposed_change: Add a mandatory Nacha fraud-monitoring control (design, annual review, evidence) as a fixed sponsor-year event and as a TPSP obligation in 14 §3. Recast §6's fraud lever as a compliance floor and not an ASSUMPTION-level saving.

target_claim_or_section: §3 OFAC row 'Must remain with sponsor (sponsor is the US person making payments)'; 04 §2/§4
challenge: Two problems. (1) OFAC obligations are not only the sponsor's. Any US person, including a US software or service company that screens, clears, holds or releases payments, is barred from dealing in blocked property or facilitating prohibited transactions. Liability is strict, so a vendor that 'triages alerts' and clears a true match carries its own exposure. The table hides this. (2) The architecture does not cover the OFAC 50% rule or non-SDN programmes: entities owned 50% or more by SDNs do not appear on SLS lists, so 'free CSL/OFAC suffice' (05 RC-05) is incomplete for foreign and fiscally sponsored grantees. A third gap: OFAC recordkeeping rose from 5 to 10 years (31 CFR 501.601, IFR Sept 2024, final 2025-03-21). Screening evidence and decision replay records need a 10-year minimum retention class, which affects RC-01/RC-02 and contract terms.
evidence: 31 CFR 501.601 as amended (90 FR, 2025-03-21, final rule 2025-04864) under 21st Century Peace through Strength Act §3111; OFAC strict-liability enforcement guidelines (31 CFR part 501 App. A); OFAC 50% guidance (2014).
proposed_change: Change the OFAC row to 'sponsor accountable; the vendor has its own direct obligations as a US person'. Require a contractual allocation of screening errors. Add 50% rule and ownership screening as a gap for foreign or intermediary grantees. Set the screening and decision record retention class to at least 10 years.

target_claim_or_section: §3 MVP 'needs no custody, no payment origination, no SOC 1 reliance at first'; G1 migration assessment; 08 §3
challenge: The wedge product, a paid migration assessment that reconciles a real incumbent export, puts donor names, addresses, fund balances, grant histories, bank details and anonymity flags in a vendor's hands before any operating contract. That raises three obligations the package does not treat as gating. (a) Data protection: Unbound is a for-profit that handles nonpublic personal financial information for a financial-service provider, so the FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR 314, with breach notice to the FTC for 500+ consumers since 2024) and bank-affiliated sponsors' GLBA vendor oversight may apply. State comprehensive privacy laws that reach nonprofits (e.g., Colorado, Oregon, Minnesota, New Jersey, Delaware) may require processor contracts and DPIAs. (b) Incumbent contract terms: confidentiality and benchmark clauses on exports. (c) Donor-privacy notices that limit disclosure. 08 mentions these in one line, but 16 still calls the wedge low-burden. The Blackbaud enforcement precedent (SEC $3m; 49 states plus DC $49.5m; FTC order), which the repo already cites, shows the cost of getting this wrong.
evidence: 16 CFR 314 (FTC Safeguards Rule, amended 2023 with notification effective 2024); state privacy statutes with nonprofit coverage (CO CPA; OR OCPA from 2025-07-01; MN; NJ; DE); repo DAF-INDUSTRY-REPORT-2026-11.md line 767 (Blackbaud enforcement). 08 §3 says real records cannot be loaded without a DPA.
proposed_change: Make a DPA, an information-security programme (WISP), a privacy assessment and an incumbent-contract review a G1 entry criterion. Add their cost (counsel and security, plausibly $30-80k plus SOC 2 Type I) to the G1 capital line. Specify that the default assessment mode is sponsor-hosted profiling with no PII egress.

target_claim_or_section: §2 G2 distribution via bank/trust distributor; 14 §2 'Low-moderate: SOC 1/2'
challenge: Selling through a bank or trust distributor makes Unbound a bank third party under the Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships (June 2023). If the activity is critical, it can also be examined directly by federal banking agencies under the Bank Service Company Act (12 USC 1867(c)). Expect bank due diligence questionnaires, rights to audit, exit and BCP requirements, concentration-risk reviews and long procurement cycles. These are not captured by 'SOC 1/2'. The research rates regulatory exposure for MD-6 as low-moderate and does not price bank TPRM or examination readiness into ER-7 or into G2's 12-36 month timeline.
evidence: Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management (FRB/FDIC/OCC, 88 FR 37920, June 2023); Bank Service Company Act 12 USC 1867(c). 12 already notes '5/5 procurement' difficulty for the bank segment.
proposed_change: Add bank TPRM and examination readiness as a cost and time line for G2's bank channel (diligence, contract clauses, possibly SOC 1 Type II from day one). Raise MD-6 regulatory exposure to moderate when it is sold through banks.

target_claim_or_section: §2 and §5; 16 G2 advisor/bank channels; whole package
challenge: The package does not mention the November 2023 proposed 4966 regulations (88 FR 77922, REG-142338-07), which are still pending, with a 2026-27 Priority Guidance Plan item. The parent repo's own report records this. The proposal would treat a personal investment adviser who manages both a donor's assets and the DAF as a donor-advisor, which bars compensation from the DAF under 4958. It would also tighten the definitions of 'distribution' and 'DAF'. That bears directly on the advisor-distributed and bank/trust channel economics (adviser compensation, RCF-style revenue share) that 06, 07 and 16 treat as structural facts. It also bears on 4967 and 4958 rule-engine scope. Finalization could change channel incentives (in both directions) and product requirements.
evidence: 88 FR 77922 (2023-11-14; FR doc 2023-24982); docket IRS-2023-0053 (249 submissions per repo); 2026-2027 Priority Guidance Plan item on §§4966/6033; repo DAF-INDUSTRY-REPORT-2026-11.md line 767.
proposed_change: Add a regulatory-scenario row to 16 §6 ('What would make this wrong'): final 4966 regs adopt the adviser-as-donor-advisor rule. Model its effect on the channel thesis (CLM-017) and add 4958 and adviser-fee rules to the rule-engine scope.

target_claim_or_section: §2 MD-5 full-service administrator; MD-7 exception service; state exposure absent
challenge: The package does not assess state charity regulation. An administrator that 'holds and releases charitable money' or receives and controls contributions for compensation may fall within state definitions of commercial fundraiser, fundraising counsel or professional solicitor. California's 'commercial fundraiser for charitable purposes' (Gov. Code 12599) covers persons who receive or control charitable funds for compensation. That brings registration, bonding, contracts filed with the AG and annual reporting across many states. Separately, state AG registry status (e.g., CA AG Registry 'delinquent' or 'suspended', which bars soliciting or disbursing) may be eligibility-relevant for some sponsor policies but is classed as an 'optional' paid input (RC-05). Uncashed grant checks (E12) are also unclaimed property in most states, a reporting duty the model does not include.
evidence: Cal. Gov. Code 12599 (commercial fundraiser definition); CA AG Registry of Charities and Fundraisers (delinquency consequences, 11 CCR 999.9.x); state unclaimed property acts (RUUPA). No mention of 'solicitation', 'fundraiser' or 'unclaimed' in the package (grep).
proposed_change: Add a state-law workstream: a counsel opinion on fundraiser and fundraising-counsel status for MD-5 and MD-7 in the top 10 states; whether state registry delinquency belongs in default eligibility rules; and an unclaimed-property event in 09 (E12 and close).

target_claim_or_section: §2 'Shared vetting evidence ... screening result at time t' and 'Unresolved conflict ... Shareable (as a flag)'; 05 RA-4; 14 'media rider if publishing'
challenge: Sharing screening results and conflict flags across sponsors is a legal question, not only a licensing one. A false sanctions or 'unresolved conflict' flag on a charity that is redistributed to many sponsors creates defamation and tortious-interference exposure. Screening results about individual officers are personal data, so cross-sponsor reuse needs a lawful basis under state privacy law and processor terms. Coordinated shared exclusion signals among competing sponsors raise antitrust and group-boycott questions, which 14 flags only for the federated model. The package treats this as an insurance rider (RC-10) and 'OQ-010 contractual terms'.
evidence: 04 §2 table (screening result and conflict shareable); 14 §2 federated row ('antitrust and data-sharing terms (counsel)'); 05 RC-10 'rider only if registry facts are published'.
proposed_change: Share only source-attributed facts. Never share derived flags or screening dispositions; each sponsor's match decision stays sponsor-specific. Strip individual-officer screening results from the shared layer. Add a counsel question on defamation, privacy and antitrust for RA-4, separate from OQ-010.

target_claim_or_section: §1 AI factor 0.6 on minutes per touch; E10 grant approval 12.25 min AI-native; 04 §6
challenge: 04 rightly keeps AI advisory, but 09 books the saving anyway: humans review AI dossiers 40% faster. The package does not test whether a review that fast is a meaningful human decision. It ignores automation bias, documentation of reasoning for auditors, and model-risk controls (validation, change management, prompt and version logging tied to the decision record). If an examiner or auditor finds 'rubber-stamp' review of AI-prepared 4966/4967 determinations, the claimed reduction in human minutes for E10 and E08 is the first thing to go. Where donor-facing AI is used for account or fraud holds, state AI laws (e.g., the Colorado AI Act on consequential financial-service decisions, delayed to mid-2026) may also add duties.
evidence: 09 §1 (AI factor 0.6 is ASSUMPTION; HYP-008); 04 §2 AI-generated assessment row; Colorado SB24-205 as delayed by SB25B-004.
proposed_change: Add a model-risk and human-review-quality control event (sampling of AI-assisted decisions; reviewer override rates) with its own minutes. Make HYP-008 conditional on an auditor accepting the AI-assisted review evidence.
